facts.statement: The Mascarene parrot is recorded as extinct in 1834.
facts.quote: extinct: 1834

facts.statement: The Mascarene parrot was endemic to the island of Réunion in the western Indian Ocean.
facts.quote: The Mascarene parrot or mascarin (Mascarinus mascarinus) is an extinct species of parrot that was endemic to the Mascarene island of Réunion in the western Indian Ocean.

facts.statement: The Mascarene parrot had red legs and naked red skin around its eyes and nostrils.
facts.quote: Its legs were red, and it had naked red skin around the eyes and nostrils.

facts.statement: Stuffed specimens and older descriptions indicate the body was brown and the head was bluish.
facts.quote: In contrast, stuffed specimens and old descriptions based on them indicate that the body was brown and the head bluish.

facts.statement: The Mascarene parrot was scientifically described in 1771.
facts.quote: The species was scientifically described in 1771.

facts.statement: Only two stuffed specimens of the Mascarene parrot exist today, located in Paris and Vienna.
facts.quote: Only two stuffed specimens exist today, in Paris and Vienna.

facts.statement: The date and cause of extinction are unclear; while 1834 is the latest record, it is considered dubious, suggesting extinction likely occurred before 1800 or even earlier.
facts.quote: The date and cause of extinction for the Mascarene parrot is unclear. The latest account, from 1834, is considered dubious, so it is probable that the species became extinct prior to 1800, and may have become extinct even earlier.

facts.statement: The taxonomic placement of the Mascarene parrot is debated, with recent genetic studies favoring its grouping with Psittaculini parrots over vasa parrots.
facts.quote: The taxonomic relationships of this species have been subject to debate; it has historically been grouped with either the Psittaculini parrots or the vasa parrots, with the latest genetic study favouring the former group.

facts.statement: The Mascarene parrot was first mentioned by French traveler Sieur Dubois in his 1674 travelogue of Réunion.
facts.quote: The Mascarene parrot was first mentioned by the French traveller Sieur Dubois in his 1674 travelogue from the Mascarene Island of Réunion, and was only described a few times from life afterwards.

facts.statement: The Mascarene parrot was scientifically described as Psittacus mascarinus by Carl Linnaeus in 1771.
facts.quote: The Mascarene parrot was scientifically described as Psittacus mascarinus (abbreviated as "mascarin") by the Swedish zoologist Carl Linnaeus in 1771.

facts.statement: The species name mascarinus references the Mascarene Islands, named after Portuguese discoverer Pedro Mascarenhas.
facts.quote: The name is a reference to the Mascarene Islands, which were themselves named after their Portuguese discoverer, Pedro Mascarenhas.

facts.statement: Early writers incorrectly claimed the parrot was found on Madagascar, leading Lesson to propose the synonym Mascarinus madagascariensis in 1831.
facts.quote: Early writers claimed the Mascarene parrot was found on Madagascar, an idea that led the French naturalist René Primevère Lesson to coin the junior synonym Mascarinus madagascariensis in 1831.

facts.statement: The genus name Mascarinus prevailed, and when combined with the specific name mascarinus in 1891, it formed a tautonym.
facts.quote: His new genus name prevailed and, when the Italian zoologist Tommaso Salvadori combined it with the earlier specific name in 1891, it became a tautonym (a scientific name in which the two parts are identical).

facts.statement: One of the stuffed specimens was purchased from the Leverian Museum in London in 1806.
facts.quote: The latter specimen was bought from the Leverian Museum during a sale in London in 1806.

facts.statement: Some authors associated an unidentified dark parrot seen in Africa by Hasselqvist with the Mascarene parrot, but descriptions differ, leading to invalid name combinations.
facts.quote: An unidentified dark parrot seen alive by the Swedish naturalist Fredrik Hasselqvist in Africa was given the name Psittacus obscurus by Linnaeus in 1758, who again synonymised it with the Mascarene parrot in 1766. Because of this association, some authors believed it was from the Mascarene Islands as well, but this dark parrot's description differs from that of the Mascarene parrot.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the unidentified dark parrot associated with the Mascarene parrot was actually a grey parrot.
facts.quote: The unidentified parrot may have been a grey parrot (Psittacus erithacus) instead.

facts.statement: Subfossil remains of the parrot were excavated from grottos on Réunion and reported in 1996.
facts.quote: Subfossil parrot remains were later excavated from grottos on Réunion and reported in 1996.

facts.statement: X-ray comparisons show that subfossil bones of the Mascarene parrot were intermediate in measurements between modern specimens and the stuffed ones.
facts.quote: X-rays of the two existing stuffed Mascarene parrots made it possible to compare the remaining bones with the subfossils and showed these were intermediate in measurements in comparison to the modern specimens.

facts.statement: The IOC World Bird List emended the binomial name to M. mascarin in 2016 to align with Linnaean conventions.
facts.quote: The binomial name was emended from M. mascarinus to M. mascarin by the IOC World Bird List in 2016, to conform with how other species epithets by Linnaeus have been treated.

facts.statement: In 2020, the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature conserved the name M. mascarinus as a justified emendation.
facts.quote: In 2020, the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature conserved the name M. mascarinus as a justified emendation of the original spelling.

facts.statement: The evolutionary affinities of the Mascarene parrot have been debated since the mid-19th century.
facts.quote: The affinities of the Mascarene parrot are unclear, and two hypotheses have competed since the mid-19th century.

facts.statement: Historically, researchers debated whether the Mascarene parrot belonged to the African Coracopsinae or the Asian Psittaculinae based on plumage and beak features.
facts.quote: Some authors grouped it with the Coracopsinae (of African origin) due to its dark plumage, and others with the Psittaculinae parrots (of Asian origin) based on the large red beak

facts.statement: A 2017 genetic study using a Vienna specimen concluded that the Mascarene parrot belonged to the Psittacula group.
facts.quote: In 2017, the German biologist Lars Podsiadlowski and colleagues sampled the Vienna specimen for a new genetic study and found that the Mascarene parrot was indeed part of the Psittacula group as suggested by Hume

facts.statement: Researchers proposed that the 2011 genetic results were likely caused by laboratory contamination involving other parrot species.
facts.quote: The researchers suggested that the 2011 genetic study had probably used a composite of sequences from two other parrot species sampled for the study (including a lesser vasa parrot), a result of contamination during laboratory procedures.

facts.statement: A 2018 study supported the placement of the Mascarene parrot within Psittacula and argued for splitting the genus.
facts.quote: In 2018, the American ornithologist Kaiya L. Provost and colleagues also found the Mascarene parrot (using the sequence of Podsiadlowski and colleagues) and Tanygnathus species to group within Psittacula, and stated this argued for breaking up the latter genus.

facts.statement: In 2019, ornithologists proposed splitting the genus Psittacula to retain the name Mascarinus.
facts.quote: the German ornithologist Michael P. Braun and colleagues proposed in 2019 that Psittacula should be split into multiple genera, thereby retaining Mascarinus.

facts.statement: A 2022 genetic study confirmed the relationships between Psittacula, the Mascarene parrot, and Tanygnathus found in earlier research.
facts.quote: A 2022 genetic study by the Brazilian ornithologist Alexandre P. Selvatti and colleagues confirmed the earlier studies in regard to the relationship between Psittacula, the Mascarene parrot, and Tanygnathus.

facts.statement: In 2024, researchers noted that confirmed phylogenetic findings might require placing the Mascarene parrot in the genus Palaeornis.
facts.quote: In 2024, the American ornithologist Brian Tilston Smith and colleagues noted that if the phylogenetic findings of Podsiadlowski and colleagues were confirmed, the Mascarene parrot would also have to be placed in the genus Palaeornis

facts.statement: The Mascarene parrot measured 35 cm in length.
facts.quote: The Mascarene parrot was 35 cm in length.

facts.statement: The Mascarene parrot had a wing span of 211 mm, a tail length of 144–152 mm, a culmen of 32–36 mm, and a tarsus of 22–24 mm.
facts.quote: The wing was 211 mm, the tail 144 – 152 mm, the culmen 32 – 36 mm, and the tarsus 22 – 24 mm.

facts.statement: In 1674, Dubois described live specimens of the Mascarene parrot as "petit-gris," a color similar to the dark phase of the red squirrel.
facts.quote: In 1674, Dubois described live specimens as being "petit-gris" which is the colour of the dark phase of the red squirrel.

facts.statement: Hume described the color of the Mascarene parrot as a dark blackish grey or brown.
facts.quote: According to Hume, this colour is a dark blackish grey or brown.

facts.statement: In 1760, Brisson published a description of the Mascarene parrot based on a captive bird, possibly the one preserved in Paris.
facts.quote: In 1760, Brisson published the following description based on a captive bird (which may have been the specimen now preserved in Paris):

facts.statement: The Mascarene parrot skull lacked a mandibular fenestra, had a broadly oval mandibular symphysis with a flattened lower margin, and a sharply angled downward symphysis.
facts.quote: The mandibular fenestra (opening at the side of the mandible) was absent, and the back end of the mandibular symphysis (where the two halves of the lower jaw connected) was broadly oval, the angulus mandibulae (the lower margin at the back of the mandible) was flattened instead of angled, and the symphysis was sharply angled downward.

facts.statement: In 1879, Forbes stated that the cere of the Mascarene parrot was covered by feathers, concealing the nostrils.
facts.quote: In 1879, Forbes stated the cere was covered by feathers which concealed the nostrils.

facts.statement: Forbes' claim that feathers covered the nostrils contradicts other accounts stating the nostrils were surrounded by red skin.
facts.quote: This contradicts other accounts that mention that the nostrils were surrounded by red skin.

facts.statement: It is suggested that the removal of the skull and mandible prior to Forbes' study may have distorted the shape of the head and nostrils in his illustrations.
facts.quote: This may have led to the distortion of the shape of the head and nostrils as indicated by the illustration in Forbes' article.

facts.statement: The two surviving specimens of the Mascarene parrot differ significantly in their coloration.
facts.quote: The two extant Mascarene parrot specimens also differ from each other in colouration.

facts.statement: Because several specimens were kept in captivity, the Mascarene parrot was likely not a specialized feeder.
facts.quote: Since several specimens were kept alive in captivity, it was probably not a specialised feeder.

facts.statement: A 1705 description by Jean Feuilley suggests that Mascarene parrots fattened themselves seasonally.
facts.quote: In 1705, the French cartographer Jean Feuilley gave a description of the parrots of Réunion and their ecology which indicates that they fattened themselves seasonally

facts.statement: The last known account of wild Mascarene parrots on Réunion dates to the 1770s.
facts.quote: The last account of wild specimens on Réunion is from the 1770s.

facts.statement: In 1834, German zoologist Carl Wilhelm Hahn published an account of a live Mascarene parrot belonging to King Maximilian I Joseph of Bavaria.
facts.quote: In 1834, the German zoologist Carl Wilhelm Hahn published an often-cited account of a live Mascarene parrot in the possession of King Maximilian I Joseph of Bavaria.

facts.statement: The Mascarene parrot was the last endemic bird species to go extinct on Réunion, preceding the hoopoe starling which disappeared in the mid-19th century.

facts.statement: Hume proposed that the brown coloration of the Mascarene parrot is an artifact of aged taxidermy, but this hypothesis is debated by researchers like Joseph M. Forshaw.
facts.quote: Hume proposed that this colouration is an artifact of the taxidermy specimens having aged and being exposed to light, which can turn grey and black to brown.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested that if Mascarinus were confirmed to belong in the genus Coracopsis, the species should be renamed because Coracopsis is the older name.
facts.quote: Además apuntaron que si se confirmaba que Mascarinus debía incluirse en el género Coracopsis, este último nombre es menos antiguo y deberían todos denominarse por el primero que es más antiguo
